disease.name: Urethritis
disease.icd_10_code: N34 (Urethritis and urethral syndrome); N34.1 (Non-specific urethritis); N34.2 (Other urethritis); A54.0 (Gonococcal urethritis); A56.0 (Chlamydial urethritis); A59.0 (Trichomonas vulvovaginitis/urethritis)
disease.category: Urological / Sexually Transmitted Infection (STI) / Genitourinary Disease

overview.description: Urethritis is inflammation of the urethra — the tube that carries urine from the bladder to the outside of the body. It is one of the most common genitourinary conditions worldwide, predominantly caused by sexually transmitted pathogens (gonococcal urethritis and non-gonococcal urethritis) but also by non-infectious causes (chemical irritants, trauma, reactive arthritis). Urethritis manifests characteristically as dysuria (painful urination), urethral discharge, and urethral discomfort, though it is often asymptomatic — particularly in women and in chlamydial infection — leading to unrecognised transmission and complications including pelvic inflammatory disease, epididymo-orchitis, reactive arthritis, infertility, and increased HIV transmission risk.
overview.affected_organ: Urethra (and adjacent genitourinary structures — prostate, epididymis, cervix, fallopian tubes, Bartholin's glands)
overview.prevalence: One of the most common STIs globally — Chlamydia: 128 million new cases/year (WHO 2020); Gonorrhoea: 82 million new cases/year (WHO 2020). Non-gonococcal urethritis (NGU) is the most common STI syndrome in men attending sexual health clinics in high-income countries.
overview.age_group: Predominantly sexually active adults aged 15-49 years; peak incidence in 15-25 year age group
overview.sex_differences: Men typically more symptomatic (urethral discharge and dysuria easier to detect). Women often asymptomatic or present with vaginal discharge, dysuria or intermenstrual bleeding — symptoms overlapping with other genitourinary conditions (UTI, vaginitis, cervicitis). Urethritis is a clinical syndrome diagnosis in men; in women, cervicitis and urethritis frequently coexist.
overview.is_contagious_note: Sexually transmitted urethritis is transmitted through vaginal, anal, and oral sexual contact; some causes also transmitted vertically (mother to neonate)

anatomy_note.male_urethra: ~20 cm long; divided into: prostatic urethra (through prostate gland), membranous urethra, and penile (spongy) urethra. Infection can ascend to cause prostatitis, epididymitis, and orchitis.
anatomy_note.female_urethra: ~4 cm long; more susceptible to ascending infection because of its proximity to vagina and anus and shorter length. In women, urethritis and cervicitis almost always coexist with STIs.
anatomy_note.clinical_relevance: Understanding anatomy explains complication patterns: men develop epididymo-orchitis from ascending infection; women develop PID (pelvic inflammatory disease) from ascending cervical infection

types.name: Gonococcal Urethritis (GU)
types.description: Urethritis caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae — a sexually transmitted Gram-negative diplococcus. Characteristically causes profuse, purulent (thick yellow-green) urethral discharge and dysuria with a shorter incubation period (1-5 days). Gonococcal urethritis has serious complications (DGI, epididymo-orchitis, PID) and is a public health priority due to rapidly emerging antibiotic resistance.
types.transmission: Unprotected vaginal, anal, or oral sexual contact; vertical transmission during childbirth (neonatal conjunctivitis — ophthalmia neonatorum)
types.asymptomatic_prevalence: ~10% of men; up to 80% of women may be asymptomatic
types.resistance_concern: Extensively drug-resistant (XDR) gonorrhoea is an emerging global threat — resistance to penicillin, tetracycline, fluoroquinolones, and increasingly azithromycin; last line treatments being challenged
types.common_in: Sexually active adults; MSM (higher rates); adolescents; sex workers

types.name: Non-Gonococcal Urethritis (NGU)
types.description: Urethritis where Neisseria gonorrhoeae has been excluded. The most common type of urethritis in men presenting to sexual health clinics in high-income countries. Multiple causative agents — Chlamydia trachomatis accounts for 30-40%; the remainder are caused by Mycoplasma genitalium, Ureaplasma urealyticum/parvum, Trichomonas vaginalis, HSV, and other organisms. Often milder presentation than gonococcal urethritis.
causative_agents_ranked: Ureaplasma urealyticum / Ureaplasma parvum (7-30% of NGU)
Trichomonas vaginalis (5% of NGU, higher in some populations)
Enteric organisms (E. coli — after anal intercourse)
Unknown/Idiopathic (30-40% of NGU cases — no pathogen identified)
types.discharge_character: Scanty to moderate, clear to mucoid (less purulent than GU)
types.common_in: Sexually active young adults; highest rates in 15-25 year olds

types.name: Chlamydial Urethritis
types.description: The most common specific cause of non-gonococcal urethritis globally. An obligate intracellular bacterium causing urethritis in men and cervicitis/urethritis in women. The 'silent STI' — approximately 50% of men and 70-80% of women are ASYMPTOMATIC. Without treatment, ascending infection causes epididymo-orchitis in men and PID (tubo-ovarian abscess, tubal infertility, ectopic pregnancy) in women. Also causes reactive arthritis.
special_features: Obligate intracellular organism — not culturable on routine bacteriological media; requires special laboratory methods
Long-term sequelae from asymptomatic untreated infection
Does NOT cause profuse purulent discharge (unlike gonorrhoea)
types.transmission: Unprotected sexual contact; vertical from mother to neonate during delivery (neonatal conjunctivitis, neonatal pneumonia)
types.asymptomatic_prevalence: 50% of infected men; 70-80% of infected women

types.name: Mycoplasma genitalium Urethritis
types.description: An increasingly recognised and important cause of NGU (15-20%) and cervicitis. Mycoplasma genitalium is associated with persistent/recurrent urethritis and treatment failure, largely because it has developed high rates of macrolide (azithromycin) resistance. It has a long doubling time and is difficult to treat. Causes similar complications to Chlamydia.
types.resistance_concern: High and increasing rates of azithromycin resistance (macrolide resistance); moxifloxacin (fluoroquinolone) is second-line treatment; resistance testing (for macrolide resistance) now recommended before treatment in many guidelines
types.clinical_significance: Major cause of treatment-resistant and persistent NGU; complications include prostatitis, epididymo-orchitis (men) and PID, tubal factor infertility (women)

types.name: Trichomonal Urethritis
types.description: Caused by the sexually transmitted protozoan Trichomonas vaginalis. In women: causes vaginitis (frothy, yellow-green discharge, vulval irritation). In men: usually asymptomatic (prostatitis/urethritis possible) — men are primarily asymptomatic carriers. A significant but often overlooked cause of NGU — accounts for up to 5% of NGU in men in some populations.
types.epidemiology: Most common non-viral STI in the world; WHO estimates 156 million new infections per year; higher prevalence in sub-Saharan Africa and parts of Asia
types.asymptomatic_in_men: 70-80% of infected men are asymptomatic but remain infectious

types.name: Herpetic Urethritis
types.causative_agent: Herpes Simplex Virus type 1 (HSV-1) and type 2 (HSV-2)
types.description: Urethritis caused by herpes simplex virus. Accounts for 2-3% of NGU cases. Characterised by very severe dysuria (often described as the worst dysuria the patient has experienced), urethral discharge, associated genital ulcers or vesicles, and systemic symptoms (fever, malaise, inguinal lymphadenopathy) during primary infection. Recurrent episodes are common (especially HSV-2).
types.clinical_features: Severe dysuria; genital ulcers/blisters; systemic features (primary infection); inguinal lymphadenopathy

types.name: Non-Infectious / Irritant Urethritis
types.description: Urethritis from non-infectious causes. Important to distinguish from STI-related urethritis as it does not require antibiotics or partner notification. Often overlooked cause of dysuria and urethral discomfort.
causes: Chemical irritants: soaps, shower gels, bubble bath, perfumed products applied to genitals
Latex condom allergy or lubricant sensitivity
Urethral trauma — vigorous sexual activity, masturbation, catheterisation, cystoscopy
Physical manipulation of urethra (fingering, sexual devices)
Detergents or fabric softeners in underwear
types.diagnosis: Urethritis symptoms with negative STI screen; history of chemical or physical exposure

types.name: Reactive Urethritis (Urethritis in Reactive Arthritis / Reiter's Syndrome)
types.description: Urethritis as part of reactive arthritis — an immune-mediated systemic condition triggered by infection (urogenital Chlamydia most commonly; also GI pathogens — Salmonella, Campylobacter, Shigella, Yersinia). The classic 'Reiter's triad': urethritis + arthritis + conjunctivitis. Also includes circinate balanitis (painless penile skin lesions) and keratoderma blenorrhagica (skin lesions resembling psoriasis).
types.associated_infection: Chlamydia trachomatis most common urogenital trigger; HLA-B27 gene increases susceptibility
types.treatment: Treat the causative organism; NSAIDs and DMARDs for arthritis; systemic management

types.name: Persistent/Recurrent Non-Gonococcal Urethritis (PNGU / RNGU)
types.description: Urethritis that persists or recurs after standard treatment. A significant clinical challenge. Causes include: antibiotic resistance (especially Mycoplasma genitalium macrolide resistance), re-infection from untreated partner, inadequate treatment adherence, Ureaplasma infection, Trichomonas vaginalis (often missed), undiagnosed chemical/traumatic cause, or true idiopathic urethritis.
types.management: Extended or alternative antibiotic courses; partner re-treatment; Mycoplasma resistance testing; Trichomonas testing; exclude chemical causes

severity_levels.name: Asymptomatic Urethritis
severity_levels.description: Laboratory evidence of urethral infection (positive NAAT, positive swab culture) without symptoms. Most common presentation of chlamydial urethritis in women and trichomoniasis in men.
severity_levels.symptoms: None — detected only through screening or contact tracing
severity_levels.significance: Despite absence of symptoms, organism is present and transmissible; complications (PID, epididymitis) can still develop; treatment mandatory
severity_levels.management: Full STI treatment; partner notification; same as symptomatic; testing for co-infections

severity_levels.name: Mild Symptomatic Urethritis
severity_levels.description: Mild dysuria and minimal or intermittent urethral discharge; minimal impact on daily activities
severity_levels.symptoms: Mild burning on urination; scant clear or mucoid discharge (especially morning); mild urethral discomfort; no systemic features
severity_levels.functional_impact: Mild discomfort; daily activities mostly unaffected
severity_levels.management: Appropriate STI testing and antibiotic treatment; partner notification; sexual abstinence during treatment

severity_levels.name: Moderate Symptomatic Urethritis
severity_levels.description: Significant dysuria and urethral discharge causing meaningful distress
severity_levels.symptoms: Moderate to severe dysuria; noticeable urethral discharge (may be purulent); urethral itch; frequent urination; urethral discomfort at rest
severity_levels.functional_impact: Significant discomfort affecting daily activities and sexual function
severity_levels.management: STI full evaluation; dual antibiotic therapy (cover both GU and NGU); partner notification; refrain from sexual activity

severity_levels.name: Severe / Complicated Urethritis
severity_levels.description: Urethritis with complications: systemic spread, ascending infection, or associated systemic illness
severity_levels.symptoms: Severe systemic symptoms (fever, rigors, widespread joint pain); ascending complications (epididymo-orchitis — unilateral testicular pain and swelling; pelvic inflammatory disease — lower abdominal pain, abnormal vaginal discharge, fever); disseminated gonococcal infection (skin rash, migratory polyarthritis)
severity_levels.functional_impact: Significant disability; hospitalisation may be required
severity_levels.management: Hospitalisation for complicated cases; IV antibiotics; gynaecology/urology specialist referral; partner management; STI contact tracing

sexually_transmitted_organisms.prevalence_in_urethritis: ~20-30% of urethritis in STI clinic attendees (varies by population)
sexually_transmitted_organisms.mechanism: Adheres to urethral epithelium via pili and outer membrane proteins; invades and replicates within urethral mucosal cells; causes intense purulent inflammation; can ascend to cause epididymo-orchitis, PID, and systemic dissemination
sexually_transmitted_organisms.antibiotic_resistance: Multi-drug resistant (MDR) and extensively drug-resistant (XDR) gonorrhoea is a major global health emergency — WHO priority pathogen; resistant to penicillins (plasmid and chromosomal), tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones (>50% resistance in many countries), and macrolides; ceftriaxone remains primary treatment but decreasing susceptibility reported

sexually_transmitted_organisms.prevalence_in_urethritis: 30-40% of NGU; most common identifiable cause of NGU
sexually_transmitted_organisms.mechanism: Elementary bodies (infective form) attach to columnar epithelial cells; enter cells and multiply as reticulate bodies; large chlamydial inclusions visible on special staining; exits by cell lysis (destructive) or exocytosis
sexually_transmitted_organisms.serovars: Serovars D-K cause urogenital infection; serovars L1-L3 cause Lymphogranuloma Venereum (LGV) — more invasive

sexually_transmitted_organisms.mechanism: Attaches to urethral epithelium via specialized tip structure; lacks cell wall (intrinsically resistant to beta-lactam antibiotics and glycopeptides); slowly replicating (doubling time ~12 hours)
sexually_transmitted_organisms.resistance: Macrolide resistance (mutations in 23S rRNA gene) in 30-60% in many countries; growing fluoroquinolone resistance

sexually_transmitted_organisms.prevalence_in_urethritis: 7-30% of NGU (causative role debated — high asymptomatic carriage)
sexually_transmitted_organisms.mechanism: May cause urethritis through urease production and ammonia generation; lacks cell wall

sexually_transmitted_organisms.prevalence_in_urethritis: 5% of NGU in men (higher in some populations and settings)
sexually_transmitted_organisms.mechanism: Attaches to urethral epithelium; causes direct cytopathic effect and inflammatory response; primarily causes vaginitis in women
Infects urethral squamous and transitional epithelium; primary infection causes severe inflammation; establishes latency in sacral dorsal root ganglia with recurrent episodes
Respiratory virus that can infect urogenital epithelium; may cause urethritis with associated pharyngitis

non_sexually_transmitted_infections: Uropathogens from UTI reaching urethra: E. coli, Klebsiella, Proteus (especially in women; anal intercourse)
Bacterial urethritis from urinary tract infection in children and elderly
Staphylococcus saprophyticus (young women — also causes UTI)

non_infectious_causes: Chemical irritants: soaps, shower gels, bubble bath, antiseptics, spermicides (nonoxynol-9)
Latex allergy or condom lubricant sensitivity
Mechanical trauma: vigorous sexual activity, masturbation, catheterisation, cystoscopy, urethral dilation
Urethral stricture (obstructs urinary flow — secondary inflammation)
Radiation urethritis (after radiotherapy for prostate/bladder/cervical cancer)
Fabric softeners and detergents on underwear
risk_factors: Unprotected sexual intercourse (vaginal, anal, oral) with new or multiple partners
Young age — highest rates of gonorrhoea and chlamydia in 15-25 year olds
Men who have sex with men (MSM) — higher rates of gonorrhoea and higher risk of multi-site infection (urethral + pharyngeal + rectal)
History of previous STIs — marker of risk behaviour
Sexual contact tracing — exposure to confirmed STI case
Use of spermicidal contraceptives (irritant; disrupt mucosal barrier)
Immunosuppression (HIV, steroids, chemotherapy) — altered mucosal immunity
Drug and alcohol use — impairs sexual decision-making
Low socioeconomic status and limited access to sexual health services
Lack of circumcision (some evidence for slightly higher STI rates)

symptoms.important_note: Urethritis is frequently ASYMPTOMATIC — especially chlamydial infection (50-70% asymptomatic) and Mycoplasma genitalium. In women, urethritis and cervicitis typically coexist, and symptoms may be absent or attributed to UTI or vaginal infection. Asymptomatic individuals are still infectious and still at risk of complications. Screening is essential in at-risk populations.

primary_symptoms.name: Dysuria (Painful Urination)
primary_symptoms.description: Burning, stinging, or painful sensation during or immediately after urination — felt along the urethra. Classically described as a 'burning pipe' sensation. In men, dysuria is often the most prominent symptom. In women, dysuria from urethritis may be difficult to distinguish from UTI (cystitis) — external dysuria (burning at the vaginal opening) suggests urethritis or vulvovaginitis more than internal dysuria (suprapubic pain on bladder filling) which suggests UTI.
primary_symptoms.severity: Mild to Severe (most severe with herpetic urethritis)
primary_symptoms.onset: 1-5 days after exposure (gonorrhoea); 7-21 days (chlamydia); minutes to hours (chemical/traumatic)
primary_symptoms.note: Herpetic urethritis causes the most severe dysuria of any urethritis type — sometimes so severe it causes urinary retention

primary_symptoms.name: Urethral Discharge
primary_symptoms.description: Abnormal fluid discharge from the urethral meatus (urethral opening). Character helps distinguish gonococcal from non-gonococcal urethritis: PURULENT (thick, yellow or yellow-green, profuse) = strongly suggests gonococcal urethritis; MUCOID or MUCOPURULENT (clear to white-grey, scant to moderate) = more typical of NGU (Chlamydia, Mycoplasma). 'Morning drop' — small amount of discharge noticed when first waking and underwear staining — is a subtle early sign of NGU.
primary_symptoms.severity: Varies — minimal in NGU; profuse in GU
primary_symptoms.assessment: Always examine the urethra by asking patient to 'milk' urethra if no spontaneous discharge visible; morning examination before first urination of day gives highest yield

primary_symptoms.name: Urethral Itch, Irritation, and Tingling
primary_symptoms.description: Uncomfortable itching, tingling, or irritation at the urethral meatus or along the urethra, without voiding. Often an early or subtle symptom of urethritis — present even when discharge is minimal. May be the only symptom in mild NGU. Patients often describe it as 'something in the urethra' or 'uncomfortable feeling at the tip of the penis'.
primary_symptoms.onset: Often the earliest symptom — may precede discharge

primary_symptoms.name: Urinary Frequency and Urgency
primary_symptoms.description: Increased need to urinate (frequency) or sudden compelling urge to urinate (urgency). Urethral inflammation causes irritation of bladder trigone (through shared innervation) — mimicking cystitis (UTI). Helps explain why women with urethritis often believe they have a urinary tract infection.
primary_symptoms.note: If urinary frequency/urgency is the predominant symptom without dysuria or discharge, consider UTI rather than STI — send MSU for culture

primary_symptoms.name: Urethral Redness and Swelling
primary_symptoms.description: Erythema (redness) and oedema (swelling) at or around the urethral meatus — visible on examination. More prominent in gonococcal urethritis. May be associated with preputial (foreskin) inflammation (balanitis or balanoposthitis).

primary_symptoms.name: Haematuria (Blood in Urine)
primary_symptoms.description: Blood in the urine — may be visible (macroscopic haematuria — pink/red urine) or microscopic (detected on urine dipstick). Uncommon in urethritis but can occur with herpetic urethritis, very severe gonococcal urethritis, or urethral trauma. Haematuria with urethritis should also prompt consideration of UTI, urinary stones, or bladder pathology (especially in older patients).
primary_symptoms.note: Haematuria in urethritis warrants urine dipstick and MSU culture

secondary_symptoms: Penile tip soreness and tenderness — especially on physical examination
Underwear or clothing staining from urethral discharge
Dyspareunia (painful intercourse) — especially in women with concurrent cervicitis
Intermenstrual or post-coital bleeding in women — sign of concomitant cervicitis (Chlamydia, gonorrhoea)
Altered vaginal discharge in women — increased volume, abnormal colour, or odour (cervicitis co-existing with urethritis)
Lower abdominal or pelvic pain in women — early sign of ascending PID
Scrotal/testicular pain or swelling in men — epididymo-orchitis (complication of ascending infection)
Perianal or rectal symptoms if rectal infection co-exists (especially MSM) — rectal discharge, rectal pain (proctitis)
Pharyngeal discomfort or sore throat — if concomitant pharyngeal gonorrhoea/chlamydia from oral sex
Fever and systemic illness — ascending complicated infection or disseminated gonococcal infection
Skin rash and joint pain — disseminated gonococcal infection (DGI) or reactive arthritis

symptoms_in_women.overview: Urethritis in women most commonly coexists with cervicitis (infection of the cervix). Women are often asymptomatic or have non-specific symptoms easily attributed to UTI or vaginitis — leading to delayed diagnosis and complications.
key_symptoms: Dysuria — may be external (burning at vaginal entrance — suggests urethritis/vaginitis) rather than internal (suprapubic — more typical of cystitis)
Urinary frequency and urgency mimicking UTI
Increased or abnormal vaginal discharge — change in colour (yellow/green), consistency, or odour
Intermenstrual bleeding or post-coital bleeding — highly specific for cervicitis
Lower abdominal pain — early sign of PID
Deep dyspareunia (pain deep during intercourse) — PID
Often COMPLETELY ASYMPTOMATIC — detected only through partner notification or routine STI screening
symptoms_in_women.clinical_tip: Any woman with recurrent 'UTIs' that do not respond to standard antibiotics, or UTI without dipstick evidence of infection, should be tested for STIs (Chlamydia, gonorrhoea)

symptoms_in_men_who_have_sex_with_men_ms.extra_genital_sites: STIs in MSM commonly affect multiple sites simultaneously — urethra, pharynx, and rectum. Pharyngeal gonorrhoea (usually asymptomatic sore throat) and rectal chlamydia/gonorrhoea (proctitis) frequently coexist with urethral infection and require testing at all sites.
symptoms_in_men_who_have_sex_with_men_ms.rectal_symptoms: Rectal discharge, anal pain, tenesmus, constipation (rectal gonorrhoea or LGV proctitis)

warning_signs_of_complications: Scrotal pain, swelling, and tenderness in men — EPIDIDYMO-ORCHITIS (requires urgent urology/GUM referral; IV antibiotics if severe)
Unilateral testicular pain that began during upper respiratory infection — possible torsion (surgical emergency — distinguish from epididymo-orchitis urgently)
Lower abdominal pain with fever and abnormal vaginal discharge in women — PELVIC INFLAMMATORY DISEASE (ascending infection; risk of infertility)
Migratory joint pain, skin rash (pustular or haemorrhagic), fever — DISSEMINATED GONOCOCCAL INFECTION (DGI)
Unilateral eye redness and discharge — possible concurrent gonococcal conjunctivitis; do NOT touch eyes after genitals
Asymmetrical swollen lymph nodes in groin (inguinal lymphadenopathy) — possible LGV (Lymphogranuloma Venereum — Chlamydia serovars L1-L3); rare; primarily MSM
Inability to pass urine despite urge — urinary retention; possible severe urethral inflammation or urethral stricture
Symptoms in a partner — possible STI transmission requiring simultaneous treatment of both partners

important_principles: Urethritis is a SYNDROMIC DIAGNOSIS — initial treatment often starts based on clinical assessment while awaiting laboratory confirmation
Always test for BOTH gonorrhoea AND chlamydia simultaneously (co-infection common in 15-30%)
Always offer testing for co-existing STIs: HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C (in MSM and PWID)
First-catch urine (FCU) NAAT is the preferred diagnostic sample in men for gonorrhoea and chlamydia
In women: self-taken vulvovaginal swab or cervical swab — FCU has lower sensitivity in women
Microscopy of urethral smear (Gram stain) allows immediate diagnosis/exclusion of gonorrhoea at point-of-care
Culture for Neisseria gonorrhoeae is ESSENTIAL alongside NAAT to enable antibiotic sensitivity testing
Partner notification (contact tracing) is a legal and ethical obligation — essential to prevent re-infection and community spread
medical_history: Sexual history: last sexual contact (date and type — vaginal, anal, oral), number of recent partners, gender of partners, condom use, new or casual partner
Site of exposure: vaginal, anal, oral (indicates which sites to test — urethra, pharynx, rectum)
Symptom history: onset, duration, character of dysuria and discharge (purulent vs mucoid), associated symptoms (testicular pain, lower abdominal pain, skin rash, joint pain)
Previous STI history: past gonorrhoea, chlamydia, or other STIs; treatment history
Partner symptoms or known STI diagnosis in partner(s)
Current medications: antibiotics (may mask infection or affect culture results), immunosuppressants
Allergy history: penicillin, cephalosporins, macrolides (essential for antibiotic choice)
Last menstrual period (women): to assess PID risk; differentiate urethritis from vaginitis
Pregnancy status (women): affects antibiotic choices (doxycycline contraindicated in pregnancy)
HIV status: affects treatment decisions and susceptibility to atypical pathogens
Travel history: travel to areas with high antibiotic-resistant gonorrhoea
physical_examination: Inspect external genitalia: urethral meatus for discharge, erythema, or ulceration; foreskin (retractable? balanitis?); ulcers, warts, or lesions
Urethral milking: gently compress the glans penis from base to tip to express discharge if not spontaneously visible; perform before asking patient to urinate
Character of discharge: purulent (thick, yellow-green) vs mucoid (clear, mucoid) — guides empirical treatment; take swab
Testicular and epididymal examination in men: tenderness, swelling, induration of epididymis (epididymo-orchitis); testicular torsion differential (emergency)
Inguinal lymph node assessment: lymphadenopathy suggests STI, LGV, or early syphilis
Skin examination: maculopapular, pustular, or haemorrhagic skin lesions (disseminated gonococcal infection — DGI)
Joint examination: swollen, hot, tender joints (reactive arthritis; DGI-associated arthritis)
In women — pelvic examination: cervical discharge and ectopy (cervicitis); cervical motion tenderness (chandelier sign — PID); adnexal tenderness; uterine tenderness (PID)
Abdominal examination: lower abdominal tenderness (PID in women; prostatitis in men)
Prostate examination in men (digital rectal examination): tender, boggy prostate (prostatitis)
Throat examination if pharyngeal symptoms or pharyngeal exposure to STI

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Nucleic Acid Amplification Test (NAAT) for Gonorrhoea and Chlamydia
diagnostic_tests.description: The most sensitive test for both Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis. A single sample simultaneously detects both organisms. Preferred test for all patients with suspected urethritis. Can be performed on first-catch urine (FCU) in men and self-taken vulvovaginal swab in women.

samples.men: First-catch urine (FCU) — first 20-30mL of urine passed (concentrated urethral washings); urethal swab also acceptable
samples.women: Self-taken vulvovaginal swab (sensitivity comparable to cervical swab; preferred for convenience); cervical swab; FCU (lower sensitivity in women)
samples.extra_genital: Pharyngeal and rectal swabs for MSM and symptomatic sites

diagnostic_tests.purpose: Definitive diagnosis of gonorrhoea and chlamydia; confirm clinical diagnosis; guide treatment
diagnostic_tests.turnaround: Same day to 48 hours depending on laboratory
diagnostic_tests.note: NAAT does not detect antimicrobial resistance — culture required alongside NAAT for gonorrhoea

diagnostic_tests.description: Urethral swab Gram stain examined under microscope. Diagnoses gonorrhoea at point of care: the finding of Gram-negative intracellular diplococci (GNID) within polymorphonuclear leucocytes is pathognomonic for gonococcal urethritis in symptomatic men. Assesses urethral inflammation by counting polymorphonuclear leucocytes (PMNLs/WBCs) per high-power field. Criterion for urethritis: ≥5 PMNLs/hpf in urethral smear or ≥10 PMNLs/hpf in FCU.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Immediate point-of-care diagnosis of gonococcal urethritis; confirm urethral inflammation (polymorphonuclear leucocytes)
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: GNID within PMNLs: sensitivity ~95% specificity ~99% for gonorrhoea in symptomatic men; ≥5 PMNLs/hpf on urethral smear = urethritis confirmed; NEGATIVE smear does NOT exclude gonorrhoea or NGU
diagnostic_tests.sensitivity_by_context: High sensitivity in symptomatic men with discharge; lower sensitivity in women and asymptomatic individuals — NAAT always required

diagnostic_tests.description: Growing N. gonorrhoeae on selective Thayer-Martin or similar chocolate agar from a urethral or cervical swab. Essential to perform ALONGSIDE NAAT because culture is necessary for antibiotic susceptibility testing (AST) — critical information for managing drug-resistant gonorrhoea. Culture requires rapid transport to laboratory at correct temperature.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: ESSENTIAL for antibiotic susceptibility testing of N. gonorrhoeae; monitoring for antimicrobial resistance; mandatory in treatment failure cases
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Sensitivity ~85-95% in symptomatic disease; less sensitive than NAAT; turnaround 48-72 hours
diagnostic_tests.instruction: Culture swab must be transported in transport medium (Stuart's or Amies with charcoal) and processed within 24 hours; do NOT refrigerate gonorrhoea culture swabs

diagnostic_tests.description: Specific NAAT (PCR) for Mycoplasma genitalium — increasingly recommended for all NGU cases, especially persistent/recurrent NGU. Many tests now also detect macrolide resistance mutations (23S rRNA gene mutations) — crucial for treatment selection because macrolide-resistant Mycoplasma requires moxifloxacin rather than azithromycin.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Diagnose Mycoplasma genitalium; detect macrolide resistance mutations to guide treatment (azithromycin vs moxifloxacin)
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: PCR sensitivity >95%; macrolide resistance mutation testing guides choice between azithromycin and moxifloxacin
diagnostic_tests.when_to_test: All NGU cases per current BASHH/IUSTI guidelines 2022; mandatory in persistent/recurrent NGU

diagnostic_tests.description: NAAT (PCR) is the most sensitive test for Trichomonas vaginalis and preferred where available. Wet preparation microscopy (motile flagellated protozoa on fresh sample) is rapid but low sensitivity (~50-70%). Point-of-care antigen tests available. In men: first-catch urine; in women: vaginal swab.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detect Trichomonas vaginalis — frequently missed cause of urethritis and vaginitis; treat with metronidazole
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: NAAT sensitivity ~95-99%; wet prep sensitivity ~50-70%; both should be considered if clinical suspicion

diagnostic_tests.test_name: HIV Test (4th Generation Antigen/Antibody Combination Test)
diagnostic_tests.description: HIV testing is integral to all sexual health consultations. 4th generation tests detect p24 antigen AND antibodies from 4 weeks after exposure. Detectable within 4 weeks of acute HIV infection. Reactive result requires confirmatory testing. Patients with urethritis from STIs have significantly increased HIV risk (disrupted mucosal barrier; inflammatory cells expressing CCR5 HIV co-receptor at infection site).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Routine HIV screening with all STI testing; detect HIV co-infection; assess HIV risk
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: 4th generation test: sensitivity >99.9%; window period: positive from 4 weeks post-exposure (virtually 100% by 6 weeks)

diagnostic_tests.description: Syphilis serological testing is part of routine STI screening for all patients with urethritis. Treponemal tests (TPPA, CLIA) detect antibodies to Treponema pallidum — remain positive for life after treatment. Non-treponemal tests (RPR, VDRL) reflect disease activity — declining title after treatment.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Routine syphilis screening; syphilis and urethritis frequently co-occur
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: CLIA or TPPA: positive = syphilis exposure (requires confirmatory testing and staging); RPR titer guides treatment response monitoring

diagnostic_tests.description: Urine dipstick for leucocytes and nitrites to screen for co-existing UTI. Urine microscopy for pus cells (pyuria >10 WBCs/hpf in FCU spun sediment). Pyuria without bacteriuria (sterile pyuria) on culture suggests STI (gonococcal, chlamydial, or herpetic urethritis) rather than standard UTI.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Screen for co-existing UTI; sterile pyuria supports urethritis diagnosis; guides differential diagnosis of dysuria
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Positive leucocyte esterase on dipstick in FCU supports urethritis; nitrites positive suggests bacterial UTI; sterile pyuria = STI or non-bacterial urethritis

diagnostic_tests.description: Standard urine culture to exclude bacterial urinary tract infection (UTI) — particularly important in women where UTI and urethritis have overlapping symptoms. A negative MSU culture in a woman with dysuria supports a diagnosis of STI-related urethritis.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Exclude urinary tract infection in all patients with dysuria; particularly important in women with suspected urethritis vs UTI
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Bacterial growth >10⁵ CFU/mL = UTI; no significant growth in urethritis (sterile pyuria)

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Hepatitis B Surface Antigen (HBsAg) and Antibodies (Anti-HBc, Anti-HBs)
diagnostic_tests.description: Hepatitis B is sexually transmitted. Baseline hepatitis B serology identifies: unimmunised patients (offer vaccination); chronic carriers (HBsAg positive — refer hepatology); immune patients (anti-HBs >10 IU/L).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Routine hepatitis B screening in STI clinic; identify vaccination needs

diagnostic_tests.description: Hepatitis C is increasingly transmitted sexually — especially among HIV-positive MSM and those who have sex involving rectal trauma, fisting, or group sex. Recommended screening at all STI clinics for MSM and people with HIV.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detect hepatitis C co-infection in high-risk populations

diagnostic_tests.description: If genital ulcers, vesicles, or herpetic lesions visible — swab for HSV PCR (much more sensitive than viral culture). First-catch urine PCR can detect herpetic urethritis even without external lesions. Essential for diagnosis of severe urethritis with external lesions.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Confirm herpetic urethritis in the presence of ulcers/vesicles or severe dysuria
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: HSV PCR swab: sensitivity >95%; culture: ~80%; do not rely on clinical appearance alone

medicines.note: Antibiotic treatment for urethritis must be guided by the identified or suspected pathogen. Treatment should be initiated EMPIRICALLY based on clinical assessment and epidemiological risk while awaiting results. BOTH gonorrhoea AND chlamydia are treated simultaneously in most settings ('dual therapy') because co-infection is common. All prescribed medications must be taken under the supervision of a licensed sexual health physician or doctor. BOTH partners must be treated SIMULTANEOUSLY to prevent ping-pong re-infection.
treatment_principles: Treat syndromically based on clinical features while awaiting results — do not delay treatment
Dual therapy: cover both gonorrhoea AND chlamydia/NGU empirically unless confirmed NGU-only
Partner treatment is MANDATORY — treat all partners concurrently; re-infection is the most common cause of treatment failure
Test of cure (TOC) is required after gonorrhoea treatment (NAAT at 2-3 weeks; culture if possible)

Sexual abstinence: advise all patients and partners to abstain from sexual activity until BOTH have completed treatment and are symptom-free (minimum 1 week after single-dose treatments; 7 days after doxycycline course)
Antibiotic resistance: always send gonococcal culture for susceptibility testing; macrolide resistance testing for Mycoplasma genitalium
Manage co-infections: test for and treat other STIs as identified (syphilis, HIV, hepatitis B, herpes)

categories.purpose: Eradicate Neisseria gonorrhoeae and prevent complications and transmission. Choice critically determined by local resistance patterns.
categories.note: Resistance to multiple antibiotic classes is a major and growing global threat for gonorrhoea. Ceftriaxone is currently the last reliable first-line treatment in most countries. Monitor resistance data and follow national/international guidelines.

medicines.name: Ceftriaxone
medicines.form: IM Injection (deep intramuscular — gluteal or deltoid)
medicines.dosage: 500mg IM single dose (UK BASHH 2019 and WHO 2016 guidelines; increased to 500mg from 250mg due to resistance concerns); USA CDC 2021: 500mg IM single dose (or 1g if weight >150 kg)
medicines.use_case: FIRST-LINE treatment for all gonorrhoea including urethral, pharyngeal, and rectal infection; safe in pregnancy (with monitoring)
medicines.mechanism: 3rd generation cephalosporin — bactericidal; inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis (transpeptidase inhibition); highly active against N. gonorrhoeae
side_effects: GI upset if oral bioequivalent used
medicines.contraindications: Significant cephalosporin hypersensitivity; caution with penicillin allergy (5-10% cross-reactivity)
medicines.penicillin_allergy_alternative: Gentamicin 240mg IM single dose + azithromycin 2g oral single dose (UK BASHH); specialist input recommended
medicines.test_of_cure: Mandatory: NAAT at 2-3 weeks post-treatment; culture if possible for antibiotic susceptibility
medicines.note: Always combine with chlamydia treatment (doxycycline) as dual therapy

medicines.name: Cefixime (Oral)
medicines.dosage: 400mg oral single dose
medicines.use_case: Alternative oral treatment for uncomplicated gonorrhoea when IM injection not available; significantly inferior to ceftriaxone IM for pharyngeal gonorrhoea
medicines.limitation: Reduced efficacy for pharyngeal gonorrhoea; NOT preferred when IM ceftriaxone available due to emerging resistance
medicines.note: No longer recommended as first-line in UK, WHO, or USA guidelines; use only when ceftriaxone IM is not feasible

medicines.name: Azithromycin (for Gonorrhoea — With Ceftriaxone)
medicines.dosage: 1g oral single dose (with ceftriaxone 500mg IM for dual therapy in some historical protocols); 2g oral as alternative in penicillin allergy (with gentamicin)
medicines.use_case: Previously used routinely WITH ceftriaxone as dual therapy; NOW ONLY used in penicillin/cephalosporin-allergic patients (2g + gentamicin); single-agent azithromycin NO LONGER recommended due to widespread resistance
medicines.resistance_note: High levels of azithromycin resistance now prevalent globally; azithromycin monotherapy for gonorrhoea is CONTRAINDICATED
medicines.current_role: Retained only in penicillin/cephalosporin-allergic patients as part of gentamicin+azithromycin combination

categories.category_name: Treatment for Chlamydial Urethritis / Non-Gonococcal Urethritis (NGU)
categories.purpose: Eradicate Chlamydia trachomatis and other NGU pathogens (Mycoplasma genitalium, Ureaplasma) from the urethra and prevent complications and transmission.
categories.note: Doxycycline is now the preferred first-line treatment for NGU and chlamydial urethritis — superior to azithromycin for Mycoplasma genitalium co-infection. Azithromycin 1g single dose was previously first-line but has been replaced due to concerns about Mycoplasma genitalium macrolide resistance.

medicines.name: Doxycycline
medicines.dosage: 100mg twice daily for 7 days
medicines.use_case: FIRST-LINE treatment for NGU and chlamydial urethritis (BASHH 2020; ECDC 2019; CDC 2021 guidelines); also added to ceftriaxone as dual therapy for gonorrhoea to cover concurrent Chlamydia
medicines.mechanism: Tetracycline antibiotic — inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by binding 30S ribosomal subunit; bacteriostatic; active against intracellular organisms including Chlamydia
side_effects: Nausea and GI upset (take with food; avoid lying down after dose)
Oesophageal ulceration (ensure adequate fluid intake with each dose)
Photosensitivity — increased sensitivity to sunlight (use sunscreen; avoid prolonged sun exposure)
Tooth discolouration and bone growth inhibition (children under 8 years — CONTRAINDICATED)
Reduces efficacy of combined oral contraceptive pill (advise additional contraception for duration of treatment + 7 days)
contraindications: Pregnancy (all trimesters — teratogenic; affects foetal bone/tooth development)
medicines.administration: Take with full glass of water; avoid lying down for 30 minutes after dose; avoid dairy products, antacids, and iron supplements within 2 hours of dose (reduce absorption)
medicines.efficacy: Cure rate ~97% for chlamydia; superior to azithromycin for Mycoplasma genitalium if macrolide-susceptible

medicines.name: Azithromycin
medicines.dosage: 1g oral single dose (for chlamydial urethritis where doxycycline is contraindicated or not tolerated); 500mg day 1 then 250mg daily for 4 days (5-day course — more effective for Mycoplasma genitalium if macrolide-susceptible)
medicines.use_case: Alternative to doxycycline when doxycycline contraindicated (pregnancy — 2nd trimester onward for chlamydia) or not tolerated; also used for Mycoplasma genitalium if macrolide-susceptible (5-day extended regimen preferred over 1g single dose for Mycoplasma)
medicines.mechanism: Macrolide antibiotic — inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by binding 50S ribosomal subunit; long tissue half-life
side_effects: QT prolongation (rare; monitor in patients with cardiac risk factors)
medicines.resistance_concern: Growing macrolide resistance in Mycoplasma genitalium (30-60% in many countries) — resistance testing recommended before use; 1g single dose associated with macrolide resistance selection in Mycoplasma
medicines.pregnancy_use: Amoxicillin 500mg TDS × 7 days is preferred for chlamydia in pregnancy (particularly 1st trimester); azithromycin 1g single dose is an alternative in 2nd/3rd trimester if other options unavailable

medicines.name: Amoxicillin
medicines.dosage: 500mg three times daily for 7 days
medicines.use_case: CHLAMYDIA IN PREGNANCY (1st trimester — preferred over azithromycin and doxycycline in first trimester); acceptable alternative for chlamydial urethritis in pregnancy when other agents contraindicated
medicines.efficacy: ~95% efficacy for chlamydia; inferior to doxycycline for non-pregnant individuals

medicines.name: Erythromycin
medicines.dosage: 500mg four times daily for 7 days or 250mg four times daily for 14 days
medicines.use_case: Alternative for chlamydia in pregnancy when amoxicillin and azithromycin contraindicated or not tolerated; lower cure rate and more GI side effects limit use
side_effects: Significant GI upset (nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps) — most common side effect class

categories.purpose: Eradicate Mycoplasma genitalium — an important but frequently missed cause of persistent/recurrent NGU. Treatment choice critically depends on macrolide resistance testing.
categories.note: Mycoplasma genitalium resistance testing is now recommended before treatment in most guidelines. Empirical treatment without resistance testing may fail in 30-60% of cases in high-resistance populations.

medicines.name: Azithromycin Extended Regimen (Macrolide-Susceptible Mycoplasma genitalium)
medicines.dosage: 500mg on day 1, then 250mg once daily on days 2-5 (5-day extended regimen)
medicines.use_case: Mycoplasma genitalium confirmed macrolide-SUSCEPTIBLE (no 23S rRNA resistance mutations detected); superior to 1g single dose for Mycoplasma
medicines.note: The 5-day regimen is preferred over 1g single dose for Mycoplasma as it reduces resistance selection pressure

medicines.name: Moxifloxacin
medicines.dosage: 400mg once daily for 7-10 days (for NGU); 14 days for PID associated with Mycoplasma
medicines.use_case: Mycoplasma genitalium confirmed or suspected MACROLIDE-RESISTANT; failure of first-line azithromycin or doxycycline for NGU; macrolide-resistant Mycoplasma genitalium (23S rRNA mutation positive)
medicines.mechanism: 4th generation fluoroquinolone — inhibits both DNA gyrase (GyrA) and topoisomerase IV (ParC); excellent intracellular penetration; active against Mycoplasma
side_effects: QT prolongation (avoid with other QT-prolonging drugs; check ECG if cardiac risk)
medicines.fluoroquinolone_resistance: Fluoroquinolone resistance in Mycoplasma is emerging; moxifloxacin failure rate increasing in some regions

medicines.name: Pristinamycin
medicines.dosage: 1g four times daily for 10 days
medicines.use_case: Macrolide AND fluoroquinolone-resistant Mycoplasma genitalium — third-line treatment; limited availability outside France and selected European countries
medicines.note: Not widely available globally; specialist STI physician guidance required

categories.purpose: Eradicate Trichomonas vaginalis from the urogenital tract. Both sexual partners must be treated simultaneously.

medicines.name: Metronidazole
medicines.dosage: 2g oral single dose (preferred — improves adherence) OR 400-500mg twice daily for 5-7 days (equally effective, fewer GI side effects)
medicines.use_case: FIRST-LINE treatment for Trichomonas vaginalis urethritis and vaginitis; safe in pregnancy (preferred treatment)
medicines.mechanism: Nitroimidazole — enters cells and forms reactive intermediates that damage protozoal DNA; active against anaerobes and protozoa
side_effects: Disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol — severe flushing, nausea, tachycardia; AVOID ALL ALCOHOL during treatment and for 48 hours after
contraindications: 1st trimester pregnancy (theoretical teratogenicity — use after 14 weeks; benefit vs risk discussion)
medicines.note: Tinidazole 2g single dose is an alternative with similar efficacy and potentially fewer GI side effects

medicines.name: Tinidazole
medicines.dosage: 2g oral single dose
medicines.use_case: Alternative to metronidazole for Trichomonas vaginalis; similar efficacy; potentially better tolerated
side_effects: Avoid alcohol — disulfiram-like reaction (avoid alcohol for 72 hours after tinidazole)

categories.purpose: Antiviral therapy reduces severity and duration of herpetic urethritis episodes. Does not eradicate HSV — which establishes latency in sacral ganglia. Suppressive therapy reduces recurrence frequency.

medicines.name: Aciclovir (Acyclovir)
medicines.dosage: Primary episode: 400mg three times daily for 5-10 days; Recurrent episode: 400mg three times daily for 5 days or 800mg twice daily for 5 days; Suppressive therapy: 400mg twice daily (long-term for frequent recurrences)
medicines.use_case: Primary and recurrent herpetic urethritis; reduces severity, duration, and viral shedding; suppressive therapy reduces recurrence frequency by 70-80%
medicines.mechanism: Nucleoside analogue — selectively phosphorylated by HSV thymidine kinase; inhibits HSV DNA polymerase; prevents viral replication
medicines.suppressive_therapy_indication: ≥6 recurrences per year; severe/prolonged recurrences; psychological impact of recurrences; partner with negative HSV serology

medicines.name: Valaciclovir (Valacyclovir)
medicines.dosage: Primary: 500mg twice daily for 5-10 days; Recurrent: 500mg twice daily for 3-5 days; Suppressive: 500mg once daily
medicines.use_case: Preferred over aciclovir for convenience — prodrug; converted to aciclovir after absorption; higher bioavailability allows less frequent dosing

medicines.name: Famciclovir
medicines.dosage: Primary: 250mg three times daily for 5-10 days; Recurrent: 1g twice daily for 1 day; Suppressive: 250mg twice daily
medicines.use_case: Alternative to aciclovir/valaciclovir for herpetic urethritis; same mechanism; good tolerability

categories.category_name: Dual Therapy — Combined Gonorrhoea and Chlamydia Treatment
categories.purpose: Because gonorrhoea and chlamydia co-infection is common (15-30%), most sexual health guidelines recommend treating for BOTH simultaneously when gonorrhoea is confirmed or strongly suspected, until chlamydia results are available.

standard_dual_therapy.regimen: Ceftriaxone 500mg IM single dose + Doxycycline 100mg twice daily for 7 days
standard_dual_therapy.indication: Confirmed or suspected gonococcal urethritis; dual therapy covers gonorrhoea AND chlamydia simultaneously
standard_dual_therapy.note: When gonorrhoea EXCLUDED (NAAT negative) but NGU confirmed: treat with doxycycline 100mg BD × 7 days alone (or azithromycin 1g single dose as second choice)

medicines.name: Ceftriaxone 500mg IM + Doxycycline 100mg BD × 7 days
medicines.use_case: Standard dual therapy for confirmed or suspected gonorrhoea — covers both gonorrhoea (ceftriaxone) and chlamydia/NGU (doxycycline); first-line WHO/BASHH/CDC regimen
medicines.note: Doxycycline ALSO provides partial activity against Mycoplasma genitalium, making this combination superior to single-agent treatment

categories.purpose: When NGU persists or recurs after initial treatment (defined as persisting or recurring ≥5 weeks after completing first treatment), further investigation and alternative treatment are required.
approach: Confirm treatment was completed correctly by patient AND partner
Test for re-infection (repeat NAAT for gonorrhoea and chlamydia)
Test specifically for Mycoplasma genitalium with resistance testing

medicines.name: Azithromycin 500mg Day 1, 250mg Days 2-5 + Moxifloxacin 400mg OD × 7 days (if Mycoplasma macrolide-resistant)
medicines.use_case: Persistent NGU with macrolide-resistant Mycoplasma genitalium; moxifloxacin as second-line
medicines.note: Specialist sexual health physician involvement essential for persistent/recurrent NGU

medicines.name: Doxycycline 100mg BD × 14-21 days
medicines.dosage: 100mg twice daily for 14-21 days (extended course)
medicines.use_case: Some cases of persistent NGU after standard 7-day course — extended doxycycline used in some guidelines
medicines.note: Evidence for extended doxycycline in persistent NGU is limited; Mycoplasma resistance testing preferred before this approach

categories.purpose: HIV prevention medication for individuals at high risk of HIV through sexual contact — particularly relevant for STI clinic patients with urethritis from unprotected sex.

medicines.name: Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate + Emtricitabine (TDF/FTC)
medicines.dosage: Daily PrEP: one tablet once daily (continuous daily dosing — >99% efficacy if taken correctly); Event-driven PrEP (2-1-1 regimen): 2 tablets 2-24 hours before sex + 1 tablet 24h after + 1 tablet 48h after (for MSM; not recommended for heterosexual or PWID)
medicines.use_case: HIV prevention in high-risk individuals: MSM, serodiscordant couples, sex workers, individuals with multiple sexual partners and inconsistent condom use; discuss at STI clinic appointments
medicines.mechanism: Nucleoside/nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) — block HIV reverse transcriptase preventing viral replication
side_effects: Decreased bone density (monitor in long-term users)
medicines.monitoring: 3-monthly HIV test; STI screening every 3 months; renal function (eGFR) every 3-6 months
medicines.efficacy: >99% reduction in HIV acquisition with daily adherence; ~85% with event-driven in MSM

categories.purpose: Symptomatic treatment for dysuria, urethral discomfort, and associated pain during urethritis treatment.

medicines.name: Paracetamol / Acetaminophen
medicines.dosage: 500-1000mg every 4-6 hours; max 4000mg/day
medicines.use_case: Dysuria, urethral pain, and fever associated with urethritis; safest first-line analgesic

medicines.name: Ibuprofen
medicines.dosage: 400-600mg three times daily with food
medicines.use_case: Dysuria, urethral inflammation, and associated pain; anti-inflammatory benefit; avoid in renal impairment or significant dehydration

medicines.name: Potassium Citrate Mixture / Sodium Citrate
medicines.dosage: As directed — typically 2 sachets in water three times daily for 2-3 days
medicines.use_case: Dysuria — alkalinises urine which reduces burning sensation on urination; provides symptomatic relief while awaiting antibiotic action
medicines.note: No antibiotic effect — purely symptomatic; effective for reducing dysuria burning; safe; use as adjunct to antibiotic treatment

medicines.name: Lidocaine 2% Gel (Topical)
medicines.dosage: Apply small amount to urethral meatus 5-10 minutes before urination as needed; also used before urethral swab procedure to reduce discomfort
medicines.use_case: Severe urethral discomfort and dysuria (especially herpetic urethritis); urethral swab pain reduction
medicines.note: Urologists may use this routinely before urethral procedures; can be offered to patients with very severe urethral pain

diet_and_nutrition.overview: While there is no specific 'diet for urethritis' that replaces antibiotic treatment, dietary and nutritional choices significantly impact urogenital and immune health. The primary goals during urethritis treatment are: adequate hydration (dilutes urine, reduces mucosal irritation, prevents UTI), anti-inflammatory nutrition (supports healing), probiotic foods (restore microbiome disrupted by antibiotics), and avoidance of substances that irritate the urethra or impair healing. Urethritis is primarily treated with antibiotics — dietary measures are adjunctive.

recommended_foods.evidence: Strong — adequate hydration reduces urethral mucosal irritation by diluting urine, flushes bacteria from the urethra, and prevents co-existing UTI

items.benefit: Adequate hydration dilutes urine concentration, reducing burning (dysuria) by lowering urinary acidity and bacterial concentration; promotes frequent urination which flushes organisms; prevents urinary tract infection (common concurrent condition); 2-3 litres/day target
items.frequency: 8-10 glasses (2-2.5 litres) daily minimum; more in hot weather

items.benefit: Natural electrolyte hydration; mild alkalinising effect on urine; reduces dysuria; anti-inflammatory; good potassium content

items.food: Herbal teas: Chamomile, Ginger, Green tea
items.benefit: Chamomile: anti-inflammatory and antispasmodic effects; may soothe urethral irritation. Ginger: potent anti-inflammatory. Green tea (EGCG catechins): antibacterial and anti-inflammatory properties
items.frequency: 2-3 cups daily; decaffeinated green tea preferred to reduce caffeine irritation

recommended_foods.category: Cranberry and Urinary Tract Protective Foods
recommended_foods.evidence: Moderate — cranberry products reduce bacterial adhesion to urethral and bladder epithelium (proanthocyanidins block fimbrial adhesion of E. coli); more relevant for UTI prevention but beneficial in urethritis context

items.benefit: Proanthocyanidins (PACs) in cranberry prevent bacterial (particularly E. coli) adhesion to urothelium via anti-adhesion mechanism; may reduce co-existing UTI risk; anti-inflammatory urinary tract benefits
items.frequency: 200-400mL unsweetened cranberry juice or 1 cranberry supplement (500mg extract) daily
items.note: Cannot treat STI-related urethritis alone; adjunctive anti-adhesion benefit only; avoid sugary cranberry juice (worsens inflammation)

items.benefit: Similar anthocyanin and polyphenol anti-adhesion effects to cranberry; powerful antioxidants; anti-inflammatory

recommended_foods.evidence: Strong for systemic anti-inflammatory benefits; supports urethral mucosal healing

items.benefit: Curcumin inhibits NF-κB and reduces pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, TNF-α) — reduces urethral mucosal inflammation; anti-bacterial properties (antibiofilm activity); anti-oxidant
items.frequency: Daily in cooking or supplement (500-1000mg curcumin with piperine twice daily)

items.benefit: Potent anti-inflammatory (6-gingerol, 6-shogaol); may help reduce urethral inflammation; anti-nausea (helpful with antibiotic-induced nausea)
items.frequency: Daily in cooking, tea, or supplement

items.benefit: Omega-3 fatty acids (EPA/DHA) reduce inflammatory cytokines; support immune function; reduce systemic inflammation; anti-inflammatory prostaglandin production

items.food: Colourful fruits and vegetables: Berries, Bell peppers, Tomatoes, Spinach, Kale
items.benefit: Vitamin C (supports immune function, collagen synthesis for urethral mucosal repair); antioxidants reduce oxidative stress; flavonoids anti-inflammatory; Vitamin A supports epithelial integrity
Allicin has significant antibacterial properties (including some activity against N. gonorrhoeae); anti-inflammatory; immunomodulatory; may reduce severity of genitourinary infections
items.frequency: 1-2 raw cloves daily or in cooking

recommended_foods.category: Probiotic Foods (Gut and Genital Microbiome Restoration)
recommended_foods.evidence: Strong for antibiotic-associated microbiome disruption; emerging evidence for urogenital microbiome

items.food: Plain yogurt with live cultures (Lactobacillus acidophilus, L. rhamnosus, Bifidobacterium)
items.benefit: Restores gut microbiome disrupted by antibiotics (doxycycline, azithromycin, metronidazole); reduces antibiotic-associated diarrhoea; emerging evidence that oral Lactobacillus supplementation supports vaginal Lactobacillus-dominant microbiome (protective against STIs in women); reduces vaginal yeast overgrowth (common after antibiotics)
items.frequency: Daily throughout antibiotic course and 4-6 weeks after

items.benefit: Multi-strain probiotic drink; more diverse Lactobacillus strains than yogurt; excellent for restoring microbiome after antibiotics
Fermented probiotic foods; gut microbiome restoration; immune modulation
items.frequency: Regular during and after antibiotic treatment

recommended_foods.evidence: Moderate — zinc is essential for immune function and wound healing; deficiency increases STI susceptibility

items.food: Pumpkin seeds, Lentils, Chickpeas, Lean meat
items.benefit: Zinc supports immune function; essential for T-cell and neutrophil activity against pathogens; wound healing; urethral mucosal repair
Vitamin D supports innate immunity including urogenital mucosal immunity; calcium; complete protein for tissue repair

recommended_foods.evidence: Moderate — alkalinising urine reduces burning sensation from dysuria

items.benefit: Potassium-rich foods help alkalinise urine; reduce acidity causing dysuria burning sensation; easy to digest if antibiotic-related nausea
Alkalinising effect on urine; reduces dysuria burning; easy to digest; anti-inflammatory
High water content — natural hydration and urine dilution; mild anti-inflammatory; supports urinary flushing

foods_to_avoid.reason: Critical warning with metronidazole: Alcohol causes a severe disulfiram-like reaction (tachycardia, severe flushing, nausea, hypotension, headache) — can be dangerous. Beyond the drug interaction: alcohol generally irritates the urethral mucosa, impairs immune function, causes dehydration (worsens dysuria), and has been associated with increased STI transmission risk.
foods_to_avoid.duration: NO alcohol during metronidazole treatment AND 48 hours after completion (72 hours for tinidazole); avoid alcohol throughout treatment course for all urethritis antibiotics to support recovery

foods_to_avoid.reason: Caffeine is a bladder and urethral irritant — directly stimulates detrusor muscle contractions and increases urinary urgency and frequency, worsening symptoms. Caffeine is also mildly acidic — increases urine acidity, worsening dysuria burning sensation.
foods_to_avoid.recommendation: Reduce significantly or eliminate during treatment; herbal teas preferred

foods_to_avoid.reason: Acidic and spicy foods increase urine acidity — worsening burning dysuria during urination. Spices can also cause mild urethral irritation as they are partially excreted in urine.
examples: Citrus juice (lemon, orange — paradoxically despite anti-inflammatory properties, increases urine acidity)
foods_to_avoid.recommendation: Reduce during symptomatic period; reintroduce gradually as symptoms improve

foods_to_avoid.reason: Promote systemic inflammation and impair immune function; high sugar intake disrupts gut microbiome (Candida overgrowth risk during antibiotic treatment); impair white cell function
Some artificial sweeteners (saccharin, aspartame) can act as bladder and urethral irritants in sensitive individuals — worsening dysuria and frequency
examples: Sugar-free products with saccharin or aspartame

foods_to_avoid.food: Dairy in large amounts (if causing vaginal Candida symptoms)
foods_to_avoid.reason: Doxycycline and other antibiotics disrupt gut and vaginal microbiome — allowing Candida overgrowth. Women experiencing vaginal thrush after antibiotics may benefit from reducing dairy temporarily while increasing probiotic yogurt
foods_to_avoid.note: Plain live-culture yogurt is BENEFICIAL (probiotics); high-fat dairy in excess may promote Candida — individualised approach

sample_meal_plan.note: This anti-inflammatory, microbiome-supportive, hydration-focused meal plan supports recovery from urethritis while on antibiotic treatment. It minimises urethral irritants and maximises immune and mucosal healing. Continue antibiotics exactly as prescribed.
sample_meal_plan.early_morning: Warm water with lemon (small amount — do not overdo citric acid; mostly for alkaline minerals) + 1 tsp turmeric in warm water or golden milk
sample_meal_plan.breakfast: Oatmeal with blueberries, pumpkin seeds, and banana (alkalinising, anti-inflammatory, probiotic-friendly) + 1 cup plain yogurt with live cultures (probiotic) + Green herbal tea (chamomile or ginger — avoid strong black tea)
sample_meal_plan.mid_morning: Watermelon or cucumber slices (hydration) + handful of almonds or walnuts (zinc, anti-inflammatory)
sample_meal_plan.lunch: Grilled salmon or mackerel (omega-3) + brown rice + cooked spinach and bell peppers (Vitamin C, anti-inflammatory) + large glass of water OR plain dal with rice + yogurt raita + beet and carrot salad
sample_meal_plan.evening_snack: Fresh pomegranate juice or unsweetened cranberry juice + plain crackers with hummus (zinc, protein)
sample_meal_plan.dinner: Grilled chicken or lentil curry (lean protein for mucosal repair) + steamed vegetables (broccoli, carrots, sweet potato) + whole grain chapati or brown rice + plain curd / kefir
sample_meal_plan.before_bed: Warm milk or plant milk with turmeric (golden milk) OR chamomile herbal tea; ensure 2-3L water consumed throughout the day

special_dietary_notes: Take doxycycline WITH food and a FULL glass of water — take in upright position; do NOT lie down for 30 minutes after (prevents oesophageal irritation); avoid dairy, antacids, iron tablets within 2 hours of dose
Take metronidazole WITH food — reduces nausea; NEVER with alcohol (severe reaction); take at consistent times daily
Azithromycin: may be taken with or without food; nausea is the most common side effect — taking with light food reduces this
Probiotics (yogurt, kefir, or capsules): take 2 hours AFTER each antibiotic dose — taking simultaneously may reduce antibiotic absorption
Women on doxycycline should use additional contraception (barrier methods) for the duration of treatment and 7 days after — doxycycline may reduce combined oral contraceptive pill efficacy
Zinc supplementation (25mg daily) may support immune function and urethral mucosal healing — take 2 hours apart from doxycycline (zinc chelates tetracyclines reducing their absorption)
Vitamin C supplements (500mg daily): support immune function and collagen synthesis; do NOT take within 2 hours of doxycycline (acidic environment may affect absorption)
Cranberry supplements or juice provide anti-adhesion benefits for urinary tract but do NOT replace antibiotic treatment for STI-related urethritis — use as adjunct

abstinence_during_treatment.requirement: ABSTAIN from all sexual activity (vaginal, anal, and oral sex) until BOTH you AND your partner(s) have COMPLETED the FULL course of treatment AND are symptom-free
abstinence_during_treatment.duration: Single-dose treatments (ceftriaxone, metronidazole 2g, azithromycin 1g): abstain for 7 days after BOTH partners are treated. Multiple-dose treatments (doxycycline 7 days): abstain until completion of full course by BOTH partners
abstinence_during_treatment.rationale: Having sex before both partners complete treatment guarantees re-infection ('ping-pong' re-infection)

partner_notification.legal_and_ethical_obligation: Partner notification is a moral, ethical, and in some countries legal obligation when diagnosed with an STI. All partners from the relevant look-back period must be informed and offered testing and treatment.

look_back_periods.gonorrhoea: All sexual partners in past 3 months (or back to last negative test)
look_back_periods.chlamydia: All sexual partners in past 6 months (or since last negative test)
look_back_periods.herpes: All recent sexual partners; ongoing discussion with regular partner(s)

methods: Direct contact (in person, by phone) by the index patient — most common
Provider-assisted notification: sexual health clinic contact tracers contact partners on your behalf confidentially
Anonymous digital notification: services like SH:24 (UK), Tell Your Partner (USA) allow anonymous STI notification by text or email
partner_notification.confidentiality: Partner notification is done confidentially — your name is not automatically disclosed; discuss with sexual health advisor

consistent_condom_use.protection: Male latex condoms correctly and consistently used reduce transmission of gonorrhoea, chlamydia, and Trichomonas by 70-85%; reduce HSV transmission by ~50%; reduce HIV transmission by >85%
correct_use: Use from start to finish of every sexual encounter
Use a new condom for each act of sexual intercourse
Check expiry date; store away from heat and sunlight
Use with compatible lubricant (water or silicone-based — not oil-based which damages latex)
Leave space at tip; squeeze out air before putting on
Female condoms (femidoms) also effective and female-controlled
consistent_condom_use.limitations: Condoms do not protect sites not covered: pubic area, scrotum, base of penis — herpes and syphilis can be transmitted from these areas

regular_sti_screening.recommendation: Annual STI screening for all sexually active individuals; every 3 months for high-risk individuals (MSM, multiple partners, new partners)
regular_sti_screening.what_to_screen: HIV, gonorrhoea, chlamydia, syphilis; hepatitis B; hepatitis C (MSM and PWID); herpes serology if symptoms
regular_sti_screening.where: Sexual health (GUM) clinic, GP surgery, online self-test kits (NHS, Bupa, SH:24, Fettle), community sexual health services

pre_exposure_prophylaxis_prep.recommendation: Discuss HIV PrEP (tenofovir/emtricitabine) with any patient at high HIV risk — particularly MSM and individuals with multiple partners or prior STIs
pre_exposure_prophylaxis_prep.note: PrEP does NOT protect against gonorrhoea, chlamydia, or other STIs — condoms still essential

personal_hygiene_and_urethral_care: Avoid using soap, shower gels, perfumed products, or antiseptics directly on or around the urethral meatus — water is sufficient for external genital washing
Choose unscented, hypoallergenic soaps if needed for general hygiene around genitals
Avoid bubble baths, bath salts, and bath oils — soak in plain warm water only
Wear loose-fitting, breathable cotton underwear — reduces friction, moisture, and heat that can worsen urethral irritation
Avoid tight synthetic underwear (nylon, polyester) during treatment — traps moisture and heat
Urinate after sexual activity — flushes potential pathogenic organisms from the urethra
Wipe from front to back (women) — prevents faecal contamination of urethra and vagina
Clean sex toys thoroughly with soap and water or dedicated toy cleaner before and after use; use condoms on penetrative sex toys
Avoid urethral irrigation or douching — disrupts natural microbial flora and mucosal defence
mental_health_and_stigma: STI diagnosis can cause significant psychological distress — shame, guilt, anger, anxiety about partner reactions, and fear about future relationships are all normal responses
STIs are common, treatable, and affect people of all backgrounds — they are not a reflection of character or worth
Seek counselling or psychosexual therapy if STI diagnosis significantly affects relationships, sexual function, or mental health
Sexual health clinics provide confidential, non-judgemental care — attend without hesitation
For herpes specifically: recurrent herpes can cause ongoing psychological distress; herpes support organisations (ASHA in USA, Herpes Viruses Association in UK) provide peer support
Partner disclosure discussions can be very difficult — sexual health advisors can provide scripted guidance for partner disclosure conversations
Remember: most partners will respond better than feared; early disclosure allows partner protection and treatment
post_treatment_follow_up: Test of cure (TOC) is MANDATORY after gonorrhoea treatment — NAAT at 2-3 weeks post-treatment at all affected sites
Return for review if symptoms persist or recur after completing treatment — do NOT re-take antibiotics without medical assessment
Re-test for chlamydia 3 months after initial diagnosis and treatment (high re-infection rate from new or untreated partners)
Annual HIV and STI retesting for all sexually active individuals regardless of symptoms
Discuss immunisation for vaccine-preventable STIs: HPV vaccine, Hepatitis B vaccine, Mpox vaccine (for MSM)
Ensure partner(s) have been tested and treated before resuming sexual activity
Test for other STIs as appropriate: HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B and C — offered at all STI consultations

urethritis_monitoring_plan.note: Urethritis monitoring tracks symptom resolution, treatment adherence, and complication detection. Test of cure is mandatory for gonorrhoea. Re-testing for chlamydia is recommended at 3 months due to high reinfection rates.

green_zone.criteria: Symptoms significantly improving within 48-72 hours of starting antibiotics; discharge reducing and clearing by day 3-5; dysuria improving substantially; partner(s) notified and receiving treatment; completing full antibiotic course as directed
green_zone.action: Continue full antibiotic course exactly as prescribed without interruption. Maintain abstinence from sexual activity until 7 days after BOTH partners complete treatment. Stay hydrated. Return test of cure for gonorrhoea at 2-3 weeks. Re-test for chlamydia at 3 months. Annual STI screening ongoing.

yellow_zone.criteria: Symptoms improving slowly or minimally after 3-5 days of antibiotics; discharge persisting beyond 7 days; partner(s) unable to be tested or treated; concern about treatment adherence; possible re-exposure to untreated partner
yellow_zone.action: Contact sexual health clinic or GP within 3-5 days. Assess adherence to treatment. Repeat STI testing (NAAT for gonorrhoea, chlamydia, Mycoplasma genitalium). Test partner(s). Consider alternative antibiotic if resistance suspected. Check for Mycoplasma genitalium and Trichomonas.

red_zone.criteria: Any of: Testicular or epididymal pain and swelling (epididymo-orchitis); lower abdominal pain with fever in women (PID); joint pain with skin rash and fever (disseminated gonococcal infection); inability to urinate (urinary retention); severe worsening pain despite antibiotics; symptoms 2+ weeks after completing treatment; fever >38.5°C
red_zone.action: SEEK URGENT MEDICAL CARE SAME DAY. Epididymo-orchitis and PID require urgent sexual health or hospital review — IV antibiotics may be necessary. DGI requires hospitalisation. Urinary retention requires emergency assessment. Do not wait for improvement with any of these features.

complications.description: Ascending infection from the urethra to the epididymis (and sometimes testis) — most common male complication of STI-related urethritis. Chlamydia trachomatis is the most common cause in sexually active men under 35; E. coli and other uropathogens in older men. Presents with unilateral scrotal/testicular pain, swelling, tenderness, and fever. Must be distinguished from testicular torsion (surgical emergency).
complications.management: Doxycycline 100mg twice daily for 14-21 days (for Chlamydia/NGU); scrotal support; NSAIDs for pain; hospitalisation if severe; urology and GUM co-management
complications.long_term_risk: Testicular atrophy; oligospermia/azoospermia; infertility in severe or recurrent cases

complications.description: Ascending infection from the uterine cervix and urethra to the endometrium, fallopian tubes, and ovaries — the most serious female complication of chlamydia and gonorrhoea. Presents with lower abdominal pain, abnormal vaginal discharge, dyspareunia, intermenstrual bleeding, fever, and cervical motion tenderness. Can be mild and subclinical ('silent PID') in chlamydial cases.
complications.severity: Moderate to Severe — major cause of preventable female infertility
complications.management: Outpatient: ceftriaxone IM single dose + doxycycline 100mg BD × 14 days + metronidazole 400mg BD × 14 days. Inpatient (severe): IV ceftriaxone/cefoxitin + doxycycline IV then oral. TOC at 2-3 weeks.
complications.long_term_consequences: Ectopic pregnancy (6-10x increased risk); tubal factor infertility (~15% after 1 episode, 30% after 2, 60%+ after 3); chronic pelvic pain; hydrosalpinx; tubo-ovarian abscess

complications.description: Bacteraemic spread of Neisseria gonorrhoeae beyond the urogenital tract. Occurs in 0.5-3% of untreated gonorrhoea cases. Two presentations: (1) Arthritis-Dermatitis Syndrome: migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis, characteristic scattered pustular or haemorrhagic skin lesions; (2) Septic Arthritis: purulent joint infection (usually knee, hip, wrist). More common in women (especially during menstruation/pregnancy) and in complement deficiency.
complications.management: IV ceftriaxone 1g daily until improvement, then oral cefixime 400mg twice daily to complete 7-day course; joint washout if septic arthritis; test of cure

complications.description: Immune-mediated sterile inflammatory arthritis triggered by urogenital infection (primarily Chlamydia trachomatis) — typically 2-4 weeks after urethritis. Classic triad: urethritis + arthritis + conjunctivitis. Additional features: circinate balanitis (painless penile lesions), keratoderma blenorrhagica (skin lesions resembling pustular psoriasis). Occurs predominantly in HLA-B27 positive individuals. Can become chronic in ~20-25% of cases.
complications.management: Treat causative organism (chlamydia with doxycycline); NSAIDs for arthritis; physiotherapy; DMARDs (sulfasalazine) for chronic reactive arthritis; ophthalmology review for uveitis

complications.description: Fibrous scarring and narrowing of the urethral lumen from chronic or recurrent gonococcal urethritis (gonorrhoea is the classic cause of post-urethritis urethral stricture). Presents with reduced urinary stream, straining to urinate, incomplete bladder emptying, recurrent UTIs, and post-void dribbling.
complications.management: Urological referral; urethral dilation; internal urethrotomy; urethroplasty (reconstructive surgery); urinary catheterisation in acute retention

complications.complication: Neonatal Conjunctivitis (Ophthalmia Neonatorum) and Neonatal Pneumonia
complications.description: Vertical transmission from mother to neonate during passage through infected birth canal. Neisseria gonorrhoeae causes acute purulent conjunctivitis (ophthalmia neonatorum) within 2-5 days — can rapidly progress to corneal perforation and blindness. Chlamydia trachomatis causes neonatal conjunctivitis (5-14 days after birth) and neonatal pneumonia (3-12 weeks) — less severe than gonococcal but important and common.
complications.severity: Severe — blindness possible with untreated neonatal gonococcal conjunctivitis
complications.prevention: Routine STI screening in pregnancy; treatment of maternal infection before delivery; prophylactic neonatal eye ointment (erythromycin or tetracycline) at birth in some guidelines

complications.description: Repeated or inadequately treated urethritis from gonorrhoea and chlamydia causes scarring of reproductive tract structures — epididymis (male) and fallopian tubes (female). Tubal factor infertility is one of the most common preventable causes of infertility globally. An estimated 10-15% of untreated Chlamydia infections cause tubal occlusion.
complications.severity: Moderate to Severe — irreversible in some cases
complications.prevention: Early diagnosis and treatment; partner notification; re-testing for reinfection; routine STI screening

complications.description: Urethritis dramatically increases risk of both HIV acquisition and HIV transmission. STIs that cause genital ulcers (herpes, syphilis) increase HIV susceptibility 5-10x. Non-ulcerative STIs (gonorrhoea, chlamydia) increase HIV susceptibility 2-5x through: (1) Recruitment of HIV-susceptible CD4+ T cells and macrophages expressing CCR5 to urethral/genital mucosal surfaces; (2) Disruption of mucosal barrier integrity; (3) Increased HIV viral shedding from genital secretions in HIV-positive individuals with concurrent STI.
complications.management: Prompt STI treatment reduces HIV transmission risk; discuss HIV PrEP for high-risk individuals; condom promotion

complications.description: Ascending infection from the urethra to the prostate gland. Chlamydia trachomatis and Mycoplasma genitalium are underrecognised causes of chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome in men. Presents with perineal, pelvic, or penile pain; dysuria; frequency; sexual dysfunction; ejaculatory pain.
complications.severity: Moderate — chronic; significantly affects quality of life
complications.management: Long course of doxycycline or fluoroquinolone (4-6 weeks for chronic chlamydial prostatitis); prostate massage; alpha-blockers for urinary symptoms

complications.description: STI diagnosis causes significant psychological sequelae: anxiety, depression, reduced self-esteem, stigma, relationship difficulties, and sexual dysfunction. Fear of recurrence, partner disclosure challenges, and impact on future sexual relationships are common concerns — particularly for herpes diagnosis (recurrent lifelong condition).
complications.severity: Moderate — significantly impacts quality of life
complications.management: Psychological support; sexual health counselling; peer support groups; psychosexual therapy if sexual dysfunction develops
