key_points: STI screening (gonorrhoea and chlamydia) is recommended for all pregnant women at first antenatal booking and again in 3rd trimester for high-risk individuals
Untreated chlamydia and gonorrhoea in pregnancy risks: preterm birth, low birth weight, premature rupture of membranes, neonatal conjunctivitis, and neonatal pneumonia

SAFE antibiotics in pregnancy: Amoxicillin 500mg TDS × 7 days (chlamydia — first-line in 1st trimester); Azithromycin 1g single dose (chlamydia — from 2nd trimester); Erythromycin 500mg QDS × 7 days (chlamydia — alternative); Ceftriaxone 500mg IM (gonorrhoea — all trimesters — safe); Metronidazole 400mg BD × 7 days (Trichomonas — 2nd and 3rd trimester — avoid single 2g dose in pregnancy)

AVOID in pregnancy: Doxycycline (ALL trimesters — teratogenic to fetal bone and tooth development; affects fetal growth); Quinolones/Fluoroquinolones including ciprofloxacin and moxifloxacin (cartilage effects in developing fetus)

Neonatal prophylaxis: erythromycin 0.5% ophthalmic ointment applied to both eyes at birth (prevents neonatal gonococcal conjunctivitis); some guidelines recommend universal; mandatory if maternal GC untreated
Test of cure after treatment in pregnancy is MANDATORY — repeat NAAT at 3-4 weeks to confirm eradication
STI-related urethritis in pre-pubertal children (under 13 years) is a SAFEGUARDING CONCERN — always consider sexual abuse; mandatory reporting requirements apply in most jurisdictions
Gonorrhoea, chlamydia, syphilis, and trichomonas in a pre-pubertal child are presumptively sexually transmitted — full safeguarding assessment and police notification required
However: some exceptions exist — neonatal transmission from infected mother (chlamydial conjunctivitis); rarely non-sexual transmission of some organisms in specific circumstances
Conduct examination sensitively; forensic swabs may be required; involve paediatric safeguarding team, paediatric GUM specialist, and social services
Treatment: ceftriaxone (gonorrhoea), azithromycin (chlamydia — doxycycline CONTRAINDICATED in children <8 years), metronidazole (Trichomonas) — weight-based paediatric dosing
In adolescents over 13 — STI urethritis is managed as in adults; assess consent, Fraser competence, and safeguarding concerns individually
MSM have higher rates of gonorrhoea, chlamydia, and syphilis than other populations — driven by higher partner numbers and condomless sex
Multi-site infection is common — always test urethra, pharynx AND rectum in MSM regardless of symptoms (extra-genital sites are frequently asymptomatic)

LGV (Lymphogranuloma Venereum — Chlamydia serovars L1-L3) occurs almost exclusively in MSM — presents as severe proctitis, not simple urethritis; treat with doxycycline 100mg BD × 21 days (NOT 7 days)
HIV PrEP (tenofovir/emtricitabine) uptake — all eligible MSM should be offered; 3-monthly STI screening recommended for MSM on PrEP
Mpox (monkeypox) vaccine recommended for eligible MSM in many countries — associated with genitourinary transmission
Hepatitis C sexual transmission occurs predominantly in HIV+ MSM and MSM who engage in high-risk sexual practices — screen annually

Syphilis rates are very high in MSM — screen with syphilis serology at every STI attendance; early syphilis (primary — chancre, secondary — rash) requires urgent treatment (benzylpenicillin) to prevent neurological tertiary syphilis
STIs in older adults are increasingly common and frequently unrecognised — healthcare providers have historically under-screened elderly for STIs
Physiological changes: urethral mucosal atrophy (postmenopausal atrophic urethritis) makes STI acquisition easier; reduced immune response; concurrent multiple medications
Many elderly present atypically — confusion, falls, general decline rather than classic STI symptoms
Atrophic urethritis (non-infective) is very common in postmenopausal women — caused by oestrogen deficiency causing urethral mucosal thinning and dryness; treated with topical vaginal oestrogen
Antibiotic interactions more common in elderly polypharmacy — check carefully
Lower threshold for hospitalisation in complicated urethritis in elderly
HIV-positive individuals: higher rates of STI acquisition; altered STI presentations; more severe and recurrent herpes; may have atypical or more severe presentations of NGU
Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) can cause paradoxical worsening of STI symptoms after starting antiretroviral therapy
Prolonged antibiotic courses may be required for intracellular organisms (Chlamydia, Mycoplasma) in HIV-positive individuals
Doxycycline drug interactions with antiretroviral therapy — check specific ARV regimen
Organ transplant recipients on immunosuppressants: careful antibiotic selection; fluoroquinolone interactions with calcineurin inhibitors (ciclosporin, tacrolimus); monitor for QT prolongation

vaccinations_recommended.frequency: 2-dose schedule (6-12 months apart) if started before 15 years; 3-dose schedule if started at 15+ years or immunocompromised
vaccinations_recommended.reason: HPV infection is sexually transmitted and causes: genital warts (HPV 6, 11 — most common STI-associated skin condition in genitourinary medicine), cervical cancer (HPV 16, 18), penile cancer, anal cancer, vulval cancer, and oropharyngeal cancer. HPV can infect the urethra causing urethral warts. Vaccination is highly effective at preventing these outcomes.
vaccinations_recommended.target: All adolescents ideally before sexual debut (girls and boys); catch-up up to 26 years; MSM up to 45 years (UK) per specialist advice
vaccinations_recommended.efficacy: Gardasil 9: >97% efficacy against cervical precancers from included HPV types; near-complete elimination of new genital warts from HPV 6/11

vaccinations_recommended.frequency: 3-dose primary course (0, 1, 6 months) for standard adult vaccination; accelerated schedule (0, 1, 2, 12 months) for rapid protection before travel or exposure; check immunity (anti-HBs level) 4-8 weeks after completion
vaccinations_recommended.reason: Hepatitis B is sexually transmitted (4-fold higher risk than HIV per exposure through unprotected sex). Essential vaccination for all sexually active individuals who are not immune. Recommended for all patients attending sexual health clinics, all healthcare workers, MSM, sex workers, close contacts of HBV carriers, and those with multiple sexual partners.

vaccinations_recommended.frequency: 2 doses, 28 days apart (JYNNEOS/Imvanex subcutaneous or intradermal); targeted vaccination programme in eligible individuals
vaccinations_recommended.reason: Mpox is predominantly sexually transmitted in current epidemics — primarily among MSM and their networks. Mpox causes genital, perianal, and urethral lesions that may be misdiagnosed as urethritis. Vaccination recommended for eligible MSM and others at high risk of mpox exposure.
vaccinations_recommended.eligibility: MSM with multiple or new sexual partners; sex workers; sexual health clinic attendees meeting criteria (varies by country and current epidemiology)
vaccinations_recommended.efficacy: ~85% efficacy against mpox; reduces severity of breakthrough cases

vaccinations_recommended.reason: Hepatitis A can be sexually transmitted — particularly through oral-anal contact (rimming) in MSM and partners. Outbreaks among MSM are well-documented. Recommended for MSM, travellers to endemic areas, and people at risk of faecal-oral sexual transmission.

vaccinations_recommended.frequency: Single dose; booster every 5 years for ongoing risk
vaccinations_recommended.reason: Neisseria meningitidis (meningococcal bacteria) can cause urogenital infections in MSM — including urethritis. Outbreaks of invasive meningococcal disease in MSM (particularly serogroup C, W, and Y) have been documented. Vaccination recommended for MSM as per national guidance.
vaccinations_recommended.note: Particularly relevant as gonorrhoea (Neisseria gonorrhoeae) and meningococcus (Neisseria meningitidis) are closely related organisms with some cross-reactive immunity from MenB vaccines

vaccinations_recommended.reason: General health maintenance; immunocompromised STI patients (HIV-positive, on immunosuppressants) particularly benefit from annual flu vaccination to prevent flu-related complications that could impair immune function and worsen STI outcomes

when_to_see_doctor: Any urethral discharge (unusual, abnormal, or purulent) — see a sexual health clinic or doctor as soon as possible
Dysuria (painful, burning urination) persisting for more than 24-48 hours without improvement, or any recurrence
Your sexual partner has been diagnosed with an STI — you need testing and possible treatment even if you have no symptoms
You have had unprotected sex (without a condom) with a new or casual partner — STI screening recommended within 2 weeks
Urethral symptoms that do not resolve within 7 days of starting antibiotics prescribed by a doctor
Recurrence of symptoms after completing a course of antibiotics
Symptoms that partially improve but do not completely resolve on treatment
Scrotal or testicular pain and swelling — possible epididymo-orchitis requiring urgent assessment
Lower abdominal pain, fever, and abnormal vaginal discharge in women — possible pelvic inflammatory disease
Pain and swelling in joints combined with skin rash and fever after genital discharge — possible disseminated gonococcal infection
Genital ulcers, blisters, or sores — possible herpes or syphilis — requires testing
You are pregnant with symptoms of urethritis or have been exposed to an STI
Annual STI screening — even without symptoms — for all sexually active individuals, especially those with multiple partners
emergency_signs: Testicular pain and swelling developing in a man with urethritis — possible EPIDIDYMO-ORCHITIS (attend emergency or urgent sexual health clinic same day; requires urgent urological assessment to exclude testicular torsion — which is a surgical emergency within 6 hours)
Sudden onset of SEVERE one-sided testicular pain without preceding urethritis — possible TESTICULAR TORSION — CALL EMERGENCY SERVICES — surgical emergency within 6 hours
Lower abdominal pain with fever in a woman with STI — possible PID with tubo-ovarian abscess — URGENT hospital assessment
Unable to urinate (urinary retention) — seek emergency care immediately
High fever >39°C with joint pain and skin rash (pustular or haemorrhagic) and urethritis — possible DISSEMINATED GONOCOCCAL INFECTION — hospital admission required
Sudden worsening of eye symptoms with red eye and discharge — possible gonococcal conjunctivitis — same-day ophthalmology emergency (risk of corneal perforation within hours)
Confusion, neck stiffness, severe headache with any STI — possible meningococcal meningitis (Neisseria meningitidis — relative of gonorrhoea) — CALL EMERGENCY SERVICES
Signs of anaphylaxis after antibiotic injection (rash, facial swelling, breathing difficulty, collapse) — CALL EMERGENCY SERVICES
Pregnant woman with urethritis symptoms and fever — possible ascending infection — URGENT obstetric and infectious disease assessment

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is urethritis and what causes it?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Urethritis is inflammation of the urethra — the tube that carries urine from the bladder to outside the body. It is most commonly caused by sexually transmitted infections (STIs), particularly: Neisseria gonorrhoeae (gonococcal urethritis) causing profuse purulent discharge; Chlamydia trachomatis (most common cause of non-gonococcal urethritis/NGU); Mycoplasma genitalium; Trichomonas vaginalis; and Herpes simplex virus. Non-STI causes include chemical irritants, trauma, and reactive arthritis. Symptoms include dysuria (burning urination), urethral discharge, and urethral itching.

frequently_asked_questions.question: How does urethritis differ from a urinary tract infection (UTI)?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Urethritis and UTI (cystitis) both cause dysuria (burning urination) and urinary frequency, making them easy to confuse. Key differences: UTI is caused by uropathogenic bacteria (E. coli in 80%) spreading up into the bladder, causes suprapubic pain and cloudy/foul-smelling urine, is detected by urine dipstick (positive nitrites and leucocytes) and MSU culture. Urethritis is usually an STI affecting only the urethra, causes urethral discharge (absent in UTI), has a normal MSU culture ('sterile pyuria'), and requires STI-specific testing (NAAT for gonorrhoea and chlamydia). Women with dysuria and 'negative UTI results' should be tested for STIs.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Can urethritis be present without any symptoms?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Yes — asymptomatic urethritis is extremely common, especially with Chlamydia trachomatis. Approximately 50% of infected men and 70-80% of infected women with chlamydia have no symptoms whatsoever. Trichomonas vaginalis is asymptomatic in 70-80% of infected men. This is why STI screening is so important — you can have urethritis, be infectious, and be at risk of complications (PID, epididymitis, infertility) without any symptoms. Regular testing is essential for all sexually active people.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Do I need to tell my sexual partners about my STI diagnosis?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Yes — partner notification is both ethically and in some places legally required. All sexual partners from the relevant look-back period need to be informed so they can be tested and treated. This prevents: them developing complications from untreated infection, continued transmission in the community, and most importantly, re-infecting you after your treatment (the main cause of treatment failure — ping-pong re-infection). You can notify partners yourself, have the clinic's contact tracing team do it confidentially, or use anonymous digital notification services. Your name does not need to be disclosed without your consent.

frequently_asked_questions.question: How long should I avoid sex after treatment for urethritis?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: You must abstain from ALL sexual activity (vaginal, anal, and oral sex) until BOTH you AND your partner(s) have completed the FULL treatment course AND are symptom-free. For single-dose treatments (ceftriaxone, metronidazole 2g, azithromycin 1g): 7 days after BOTH partners are treated. For multi-day courses (doxycycline 7 days): until the complete course is finished by both partners. Having sex before treatment is complete — even once — virtually guarantees re-infection. The most common cause of 'treatment failure' is re-infection from an incompletely treated partner.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is the difference between gonococcal and non-gonococcal urethritis?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Gonococcal urethritis (GU) is caused specifically by Neisseria gonorrhoeae — typically causing profuse, purulent (thick, yellow-green), abundant discharge with more severe dysuria, and a shorter incubation (1-5 days). Non-gonococcal urethritis (NGU) refers to all urethritis where gonorrhoea has been excluded — most commonly caused by Chlamydia trachomatis, Mycoplasma genitalium, Ureaplasma, or Trichomonas. NGU typically causes scanty, mucoid, or clear discharge with milder or absent symptoms. Both require treatment but different antibiotics — this is why the distinction matters clinically.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Why has my urethritis come back after treatment?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Persistent or recurrent urethritis after treatment has several common causes: (1) Re-infection from an untreated or inadequately treated partner — the most common cause; (2) Antibiotic resistance — particularly Mycoplasma genitalium macrolide resistance (30-60% of strains in many countries); (3) Incomplete treatment adherence — missing doses; (4) Missed co-infection — Trichomonas vaginalis or Mycoplasma genitalium not initially tested for; (5) New sexual exposure during or after treatment; (6) Antibiotic-resistant gonorrhoea. Return to your sexual health clinic — repeat testing including Mycoplasma genitalium with resistance testing, and partner re-evaluation are essential.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Is gonorrhoea becoming untreatable due to antibiotic resistance?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Gonorrhoea resistance is a serious and growing global health emergency — WHO classifies N. gonorrhoeae as a 'Priority 2: High' drug-resistant pathogen. Gonorrhoea has developed resistance to penicillins, tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones (>50% resistance in many countries), and increasingly azithromycin. Ceftriaxone injection is currently the last reliable first-line treatment in most countries — but strains with reduced ceftriaxone susceptibility and a small number of ceftriaxone-resistant strains have been reported globally. This is why: culture for antibiotic sensitivity testing is now mandatory alongside NAAT; higher doses of ceftriaxone are now recommended; test of cure is required after every treatment; and dual therapy with azithromycin was used (though now largely discontinued due to resistance). Urethritis and gonorrhoea must be treated promptly by a specialist.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is Mycoplasma genitalium and why does it matter?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Mycoplasma genitalium is a tiny bacterium (the smallest self-replicating organism known) that causes 15-20% of non-gonococcal urethritis (NGU) and is associated with persistent/recurrent urethritis, epididymitis, PID, and possibly infertility. It is critically important because it has developed very high rates of resistance to macrolide antibiotics (azithromycin) — 30-60% of strains in many countries are macrolide-resistant. This means the previous standard treatment (azithromycin 1g single dose) often fails for Mycoplasma urethritis. Current guidelines recommend: testing for Mycoplasma genitalium with resistance testing before choosing treatment; doxycycline for initial NGU; and moxifloxacin for macrolide-resistant strains. It is a major driver of antibiotic resistance in sexual health.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Can urethritis cause infertility?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Yes — untreated or inadequately treated urethritis from gonorrhoea and chlamydia can cause infertility in both men and women. In women: ascending infection causes pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) — scarring of the fallopian tubes. Each episode of PID carries a 15% chance of tubal factor infertility; 3 episodes give ~60%+ risk. Chlamydia is a leading cause of preventable infertility globally. In men: ascending infection causes epididymo-orchitis — recurrent episodes can cause epididymal obstruction, azoospermia, and male infertility. Silent (asymptomatic) chlamydial infection can cause this damage without any warning symptoms — reinforcing the importance of regular STI screening.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is the role of probiotics during antibiotic treatment for urethritis?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Probiotics are beneficial during antibiotic treatment for urethritis. Antibiotics (especially doxycycline, azithromycin, metronidazole) disrupt the gut microbiome, causing antibiotic-associated diarrhoea and, in women, vaginal microbiome disruption (increasing risk of yeast infection/thrush and bacterial vaginosis). Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG and Saccharomyces boulardii supplementation reduce antibiotic-associated diarrhoea. For women, maintaining a Lactobacillus-dominant vaginal microbiome through oral probiotics and probiotic yogurt is beneficial during and after antibiotic treatment. Take probiotics 2 hours apart from antibiotic doses.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Are condoms effective against urethritis and STIs?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Yes — male latex condoms correctly and consistently used provide substantial protection: 70-85% reduction in gonorrhoea and chlamydia transmission; >85% reduction in HIV transmission; ~50% reduction in herpes transmission; near-complete protection against syphilis when lesion is covered. However, condoms are not 100% effective because they can slip or break, do not cover all exposed skin (herpes and syphilis can transmit from uncovered skin at the base of the penis or scrotum), and the protection level depends entirely on consistent correct use from start to finish of every sexual encounter. Condoms remain the single most effective STI prevention measure available.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What should I do if I was exposed to an STI recently?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: If you have had unprotected sex with a new or casual partner: (1) Get tested — attend a sexual health clinic as soon as possible; testing is best 2 weeks after potential exposure (allows incubation of most STIs); (2) HIV PEP: if you are HIV-negative and may have been exposed to HIV, see a doctor within 72 hours (ideally within 24 hours) — post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is >80% effective if started within 72 hours of HIV exposure; (3) Emergency contraception: if unintended pregnancy is a concern — up to 72-120 hours after unprotected sex; (4) Hepatitis B prophylaxis: post-exposure hepatitis B vaccine within 48 hours if non-immune; (5) Abstain from sex until testing is complete and results are clear.
